paper_title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Robotic manipulation demands both semantic understanding and fine-grained spatial reasoning. policy must identify what an instruction refers to, infer where the target lies, and determine how the gripper should move relative to it. This raises fundamental question for vision-language-action (VLA) models: should action prediction rely only on the final visual representation, or also on the intermediate visual computation? Most existing VLAs make this choice implicitly. Images are first compressed by pretrained vision encoders, such as CLIP, SigLIP, or DINOv2 (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2023), before the resulting features are passed to the language backbone and action model (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025). This interface exposes the encoder output while hiding the visual hierarchy that produced it. Growing evidence suggests that this separation may constrain embodied control: visual processing is critical to VLA performance (Zhang et al., 2026b), visual components are disproportionately sensitive to pruning (Zhang et al., 2026a), and action fine-tuning can degrade pretrained visual representations (Kachaev et al., 2025). We instead reconsider the interface itself, enabling action prediction to directly exploit the evolving visual representations within the backbone. We introduce NEO-VLA, structurally native VLA policy built directly on pixels and words, requiring no separately pretrained vision encoder, image codebook, or autoencoder. Following encoder-free models (Bavishi et al., 2023; Diao et al., 2024; 2025; 2026a;c), lightweight convolutional patch embedder maps raw pixels 1 Figure 1: Three VLA designs: encoder-based vs. encoder-free backbones, and discrete vs. continuous actions. (a) separate visual encoder converts pixels into image features, which are consumed by the language backbone together with text tokens; actions are generated as discrete tokens. (b) The same encoder-based visual interface is retained, while separate action head predicts continuous actions conditioned on the backbone. (c) NEO-VLA removes the separately pretrained visual encoder: lightweight patch embedder maps pixels directly into the backbone token space, while text tokens enter the backbone jointly. narrow action expert then reads cached keys and values from selected backbone layers and predicts flow-matching velocity field. into the backbone token space, where image patches and instruction words are processed jointly within single holistic architecture in Figure 1. flow-matching action expert then reads cached keys and values from diverse backbone layers with different representation hierarchies to predict continuous action chunks. This design makes visual readout depth an explicit policy choice: the action expert can draw from early, late, or multiple stages of visual computation without introducing separate visual pathway. In conventional encoderbased VLAs, by contrast, accessing different language-backbone layers still places the policy downstream of fixed visual endpoint. NEO-VLA thus enables direct investigation of where action-relevant visual information emerges and which stages of visual computation are most valuable for control. Our analysis reveals clear depth-dependent pattern. With the backbone frozen, readouts that include early layers consistently outperform those restricted to later representations; after full fine-tuning, combining early and late features performs best. Targeted interventions lead to the same conclusion: swapping early-layer activations across observations induces substantially larger prediction errors than perturbing later layers. Together, these results indicate that action-critical information emerges well before the final representations, when fine-grained spatial and geometric cues remain more directly accessible. Preserving access to these intermediate computations therefore provides strong basis for precise and generalizable control. We further compare NEO-VLA with Qwen3-VL-2B and Gemma-3-4B, which offer comparable understanding capabilities, using the same action expert and robot-training corpus. NEO-VLA consistently achieves higher LIBERO success rates under both frozen-backbone and full-finetuning settings, with the advantage particularly pronounced when the backbone is frozen and policy learning must rely directly on pretrained visual representations. Although differences in pretraining and model capacity preclude attributing the gains solely to encoder removal, these results establish the native backbone as strong and transferable foundation for action learning. We then evaluate NEO-VLA on LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, covering both standard manipulation and challenging distribution shifts in visual appearance, language, and environment. NEO-VLA achieves strong in-distribution performance while maintaining robust control under these shifts, with particularly pronounced gains under camera perturbations and image noise. These results complement the layer-wise analysis by showing that preserving access to intermediate visual computation is not only useful in controlled ablations, but also translates into practical robustness across diverse manipulation settings. Taken together, our findings point to broader principle for embodied intelligence: effective control depends not only on what the backbone represents, but also on which stages of its visual computation remain accessible to action. Our main contributions are summarised as follows. structurally native VLA policy. We introduce NEO-VLA, which combines lightweight pixelto-token embedder, shared vision-language backbone, and flow-matching action expert with configurable access to backbone layers with diverse visual hierarchies. systematic empirical study of action readout depth. Layer-map comparisons with matched expert capacity, together with attachment-point interventions, show that early visual representations are pretty effective for control, particularly when the backbone is frozen. Evaluation across backbone families and manipulation benchmarks. We compare native and encoder-based backbones using the same action-expert design and robot-training corpus, and show strong performance on LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, and RoboTwin 2.0.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Vision-Language-Action Models. Existing VLA policies typically attach an action decoder to pretrained vision-language model. Early systems emit actions as discrete text tokens (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024), while later work uses continuous diffusion or flow-matching decoders over backbone features (Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025); Team et al. (2024) instead trains transformer policy from scratch with diffusion head. Our design differs along two axes: whether the visual pathway introduces separately pretrained vision encoder, and whether actions are represented discretely or continuously. Most prior work has focused on the action side while leaving the visual pathway largely unchanged. Images are commonly processed by pretrained encoders such as CLIP, SigLIP, or DINOv2 (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2023), often at fixed resolution and sometimes with the encoder frozen during policy training. Recent studies suggest that this front end can limit control: Zhang et al. (2026b) identify the visual module as major bottleneck, Zhang et al. (2026a) find the vision encoder, language backbone, and projector among the components most sensitive to pruning, and Kachaev et al. (2025) show that action finetuning can degrade visual representations. Recent unified systems also tend to preserve the visual front end, adding modality-specific experts for generation, foresight, or world modelling above shared attention stream (Liang et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Lv et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026; Cen et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Zhang et al. (2026c) instead adds second visual pathway, arguing that one encoder may not serve both language grounding and control well. Our focus is different: we vary the visual pathway itself while keeping the action expert, the layers it reads, the training data. Native Multimodal Models. separate line of work removes the vision encoder itself, mapping pixels through lightweight learned patch embedder directly into the language backbone (Bavishi et al., 2023; Diao et al., 2024; 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2026a;c;d;b; Lab, 2026). In this literature, native can refer to different ideas: removing separate vision module, training multimodally from the start (Tong et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026), or preserving the backbones original format and objectives during policy training (Ma et al., 2026). We use the term only in the structural sense: no separately trained vision module, image codebook, or autoencoder. Control models have evolved along related lines. Wang et al. (2026) represent vision, language, and action as unified discrete token sequences, and Xie et al. (2026) replace the transformer-based vision encoder with convolutional alternative. Concurrent work studies understanding and generation without separately trained vision module (Wu et al., 2026). Our focus is narrower: we compare visual pathways under matched action expert and study which backbone depths the expert should read.

sections.title: 3 MODEL
sections.content: 3.1 STRUCTURALLY NATIVE VISUAL INTERFACE Following NEO (Diao et al., 2026a), NEO-VLA adopts structurally native visual interface that projects raw images directly into the backbone token space through lightweight two-stage convolutional embedder with an overall stride of 32, producing one visual token for each 32 32 image region. Visual and language tokens are then jointly processed throughout the decoder backbone, while continuous actions are generated by flow-matching expert, avoiding explicit action tokenization. Besides, we employ Native Rotary Position Embedding (Diao et al., 2026a) to factorize positions into temporal, height, and width coordinates with decoupled rotary frequencies. Note that image tokens retain explicit two-dimensional spatial coordinates, while videos additionally advance along the temporal axis, enabling unified treatment of images, videos, and interleaved multimodal sequences. The backbone further adopts modality-aware multimodal attention: text tokens follow causal attention, while visual tokens interact bidirectionally within each visual block. This enables dense spatial modeling while visual and linguistic representations co-evolve across layers. Consequently, the action expert can read from different stages of the visual hierarchy from fine-grained early features to more semantic later representations, rather than being restricted to single, fixed encoder output. Notably, we train the 40-layer encoder-free vision-language backbone with 2B parameters through three-stage training. We first establish visual perception through large-scale image-text pretraining while preserving the linguistic capabilities of the pretrained language model. Mid-training then deepens vision-language alignment using diverse captioning, conversation, OCR, and detection data, followed by supervised instruction tuning on high-quality multimodal interactions. This gradually advances the model from multimodal perception to reasoning, yielding strong foundation for downstream action learning. Figure 2: NEO-VLA: pixels in, continuous actions out. Previous and current multi-view observations preserve their aspect ratios within fixed token budget and enter patch embedder shared across time and views. The visual path uses no vision transformer, autoencoder, or vector-quantised codebook. Shared MLPs embed camera intrinsics and rotations, while state MLPs embed previous and current robot states. These tokens join structured prompt describing control frequency, embodiment, frame reference, and task instruction. separate, narrow, randomly initialised action expert jointly attends to cached prefix keys and values from selected backbone layers and its own action-token keys and values. Its suffix embeddings combine projected noisy actions and flow time τ with additive step, frame, and identity embeddings. Both arm blocks and the body block share temporal rotary offsets 029, with identity embeddings distinguishing the blocks. Trained by flow matching, the expert predicts velocity field that covers both arm and body action chunks. 3.2 MULTIMODAL PREFIX In Figure 2, NEO-VLA converts robot observations into unified multimodal prefix composed of previous and current multi-view images, structured language, and robot states. Each temporal block contains up to three camera views, with every view represented by camera-identity token, projected camera geometry, and patch-level visual tokens. Camera intrinsics and rotations are encoded by lightweight geometry MLPs, while single patch embedder is shared across all cameras, views, and time steps. Images preserve their native aspect ratios and are dynamically patchified under fixed budget of up to 88 visual tokens per view, with padded positions masked from attention. This design keeps the visual pathway fully native: pixels enter the language backbone directly, without an external vision transformer, autoencoder, or discrete visual tokenizer. The visual blocks are followed by structured prompt specifying the control frequency, robot embodiment, gripper configuration, action-frame reference, and task instruction. Robot proprioception is represented by six additional tokens corresponding to the previous and current states of Arm 0, Arm 1, and the shared body. State MLPs jointly encode the measured values and their validity masks, while additive embeddings identify temporal role and arm/body identity. Components absent from particular embodiment are simply masked, allowing the same token interface to accommodate different robot configurations. All prefix tokens are processed jointly by the native backbone using three-dimensional rotary positions over time, height, and width. Visual tokens from the same image share temporal coordinate, while their spatial coordinates follow the corresponding patch grid; text and state tokens advance along the temporal axis with zero spatial coordinates. Rather than collapsing this computation into single final visual representation, NEO-VLA exposes the layer-wise keys and values of the backbone directly to lightweight action expert. The expert then combines this multimodal prefix with noisy action tokens and flow time τ , augmented by step, frame, and identity embeddings, to model action chunks for both arms and the body. The three action blocks share temporal rotary offsets over the prediction horizon, while identity embeddings distinguish their semantic roles. Note that the expert predicts unified velocity field over the continuous action trajectory. 3.3 ACTION READOUT ACROSS VISUAL DEPTHS The action expert reads from configurable subset of backbone layers. Let = (m1, . . . , md) denote the layer map, where expert layer attends to the cached keys and values from backbone layer mj. (2024), NEO-VLA uses separate action expert to predict continuous action chunks. Each expert layer jointly attends to prefix keys and values cached at its mapped backbone layer and to the action tokens own keys and values. The prefix contains the camera observations and geometry, language instruction, and robot state. During full fine-tuning, the action loss updates both the backbone and the expert. Each target contains an arm chunk in R23026 and shared body chunk in R308. Each arm has 7 joint targets, 3 translation increments, 3 rotation-vector increments, 1 gripper value, and 12 hand-joint targets. The body has 3 base-motion, 3 torso, and 2 head channels. End-effector increments are expressed in centimetres and radians per step, in camera or robot-base frame. Joint and hand targets are absolute, and body actions use the robot-base frame. Targets are normalized per embodiment. Given a, we sample Gaussian noise ϵ (0, I) and time τ = 0.999u, where Beta(1, 1.5). On valid dimensions, we construct aτ = (1 τ )ϵ + τ a. The expert predicts the velocity vθ(aτ , τ, C) with target aϵ. We mask missing steps and channels, and exclude target groups that fall outside the normalization range. The training objective balances four action groups: end-effector motion and gripper, arm joints, hand joints, and body actions, with weights wg = (2, 1, 1, 1). Let ℓg denote the mean squared velocity error over valid entries in group g, and let be the set of groups with valid supervision. We minimize the training objective as follows: (1) Laction = (cid:34) (cid:80) gG wgℓg (cid:80) gG wg (cid:35) . (2) Samples without valid targets contribute zero loss. During inference, we solve the learned flow from τ = 0 to 1 using 10 Euler steps while keeping the prefix KV cache fixed. The resulting action chunk is then de-normalized back to the original action space for execution. We do not apply classifier-free guidance.

sections.title: 4 TRAINING
sections.content: 4.1 PRETRAIN DATA OVERVIEW In Table 1, we build the pretrain data from AgiBot-World (Team, 2026), Bimanual YAM (Fang et al., 2026), RoboCOIN (Wu et al., 2025b), Open X-Embodiment (OXE Team et al., 2023), Galaxea Open-World (Team, 2025a), RH20T (Fang et al., 2024), RoboMIND (Wu et al., 2025a), InternData-A1 (contributors, 2025), and DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), covering diverse embodiments, tasks, and visual conditions. 5 Figure 3: Data quality filtering. Illustrative checks cover implausible joint readings, unreliable channels, action outliers, corrupt episodes, and camera calibration, removing only affected data. Joint and projection checks are source-specific; episode retention is determined in the final corpus pass. 4.2 DATA PIPELINE We first apply source checks to exclude unreliable measurements and corrupt episodes in Figure 3. Joint readings outside 2π, or more than π from five-row local median, are marked invalid. Joint and hand channels that remain constant throughout at least 90% of datasets recorded episodes are masked. Unresolved joint discontinuities larger than π are masked for the corresponding embodiment. Action outliers are checked against expanded per-embodiment bounds; an out-of-band or non-finite value masks only its field group at that step, leaving other targets available. Episodes with missing or unreadable data, inconsistent record shapes, invalid recorded values, or too few steps are dropped. We also check camera calibration where the required signals are available. Recorded 3D arm positions are projected using the intrinsics and full camera pose. We score image motion at the projected points relative to motion over the image, and compare scores with wrong-pose controls. Untrusted poses are marked unknown while their episodes remain. Intrinsics undergo separate checks for focal length, principal point, field of view and consistency with the stored image size. 4.3 TRAINING DETAILS Our training recipe has three progressive stages. In stage 1, we freeze the pretrained vision-language backbone and train the action expert and conditioning modules. This stage uses 113,400 optimizer steps, global batch size of 8192, and peak learning rate of 2 104. In stage 2, we unfreeze the full model and continue training on the same robot pretrain corpus for 75,000 steps with the same batch size. The action expert and conditioning modules use peak learning rate of 2 104, while the vision-language parameters use 5 105. We co-train with multi-modal understanding data to retain vision-language perception and reasoning capabilities. Packed understanding examples are added on every other optimizer step, with an auxiliary next-token prediction loss weighted by 0.1 on those steps. In stage 3, we continue the full-parameter finetune initialized from stage-2 with our in-house action data for another 75,000 steps with the same batch size, all the other settings are consistent with stage-2. Both stages use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108 and weight decay 1010. Learning rates increase linearly over 2,000 warmup steps, then follow cosine decay to 10% of their respective peaks. We use bfloat16 mixed precision and clip the gradient norm at 1.0.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We organize the experiments around four questions. First, what does native-input backbone bring over encoder-based ones under matched settings (5.1)? Second, which depths does the action expert read, and what does it extract from them (5.2)? Third, how does retaining multimodal understanding affect action learning (5.3)? Finally, how does NEO-VLA perform on inand out-of-distribution benchmarks (5.4)? 6 Table 2: Backbone comparison on LIBERO. Success rates (%) at the final 30,000-step checkpoint, averaged over 2,000 episodes. Size refers to the backbone, excluding the action expert. Frozen updates only the expert; full FT updates the whole stack. Native-input rows use the linear-depth layer map. Encoder unfrozen updates the vision encoder and action expert with other layers frozen.

sections.title: 5.1 WHAT THE NATIVE-INPUT BACKBONE BRINGS TO NEO-VLA?
sections.content: We compare the native-input backbone of NEO-VLA with Qwen3-VL-2B (Bai et al., 2025) and Gemma3-4B (Team, 2025b) to examine how effectively their representations support policy learning. For fair comparisons, all the models are pretrained with Open X-Embodiment for 75k iters under the same setting. Table 2 reports frozen-backbone training, which updates only the action expert, and full fine-tuning, which updates both the backbone and expert. Results use the final 30,000-step checkpoints, with 500 episodes per LIBERO suite. Pretraining configurations and action-expert construction are detailed in the appendix. The clearest benefit of the native backbone appears before backbone adaptation. With only its action expert trained, NEO-VLA reaches 90.9% average success, compared with 79.5% for Qwen3-VL and 84.5% for Gemma-3. Its frozen-backbone score is also comparable to both fully fine-tuned encoder-based models. On LIBERO-Long, it reaches 85.4%, exceeding their full-FT results. This suggests that the native backbone already provides representations the expert can use effectively for control, reducing the need to reshape the backbone during policy learning. Full fine-tuning provides improvements, bringing the average to 95.3%. Table 3: Direct encoder access in Qwen3-VL. Average LIBERO success (%) with the same setting. Encoder access adds no parameters. Direct access to visual features alone does not reproduce this advantage. In separate Qwen3-VL experiment, we route 13 expert layers to intermediate vision-tower features. Table 3 compares this interface under the same setting. Encoder access lowers frozenbackbone performance from 79.5% to 64.9%, while full fine-tuning brings the two interfaces to similar scores, 90.9% and 90.8%. These results highlight the importance of how representations are presented to, and aligned with, demonstrating that the action expert only access to the intermediate features is not sufficient. Taken together, the results support practical contribution of NEOs native backbone: its low-level representations that transfer well to action related tasks naturally, while retaining room for improvement through full fine-tuning. Frozen backbone Full FT Original interface Encoder access Adaptation 79.5 90.8 64.9 90.9 Finding. NEOs advantage lies not simply in accessing earlier visual features, but in how encoder-free pretraining shapes them into control-ready representations. Its frozen backbone already transfers strongly to policy learning, whereas direct access to intermediate encoder features fails to reproduce this benefit. 5.2 WHICH BACKBONE LAYERS DOES THE ACTION EXPERT USE? For fair comparison, all NEO variants evaluated in this subsection are pretrained on Open X-Embodiment for 75k iterations under identical training settings. Access to early layers. sections.title: 5.3 HOW MULTI-MODAL UNDERSTANDING AFFECT ACTION POLICY TRAINING?
sections.content: VLA post-training typically either fine-tunes on action data alone or co-trains with general understanding data. Table 6 compares the two against the checkpoint before post-training. Co-training with common understanding corpora keeps understanding within 1.5 points of the baseline on MMBench-EN (Liu et al., 2023b), RealWorldQA (xAI, 2024), AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016), TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019) and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), and reaches 69.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 clean-torandomized (C2R). Action-only fine-tuning loses the ability to produce valid text, and its policy falls to 10.7% on C2R. Cotraining therefore preserves the backbones understanding and gives the strongest policy under scene randomization. Table 6: Preserving multimodal understanding enables robust VLA posttraining. Understanding scores (%) and RoboTwin 2.0 clean-to-randomized (C2R) success (%) before post-training (Baseline), after co-training with diverse understanding corpus (+ Co-training), and after action-only fine-tuning (+ Action-only). These tasks are designed to test both fine-grained manipulation precision and long-horizon execution. For each task, models are fine-tuned on only 50 demonstration episodes and evaluated over 20 trials, including 10 in-domain trials and 10 out-of-domain trials. 10 Figure 6: Real-world NEO-VLA demonstrations. (a) Pick up paper cup and pour water into glass. (b) Place tennis ball on can. (c) Place tape roll in bowl, then place the ball inside the roll. (d) Reorient horizontal can and insert it upright into tape roll. (e) Pick four gunkan sushi pieces, one at time, from table of mixed sushi and place them on plate. Frames are arranged chronologically from left to right, with dashed circles highlighting key interaction moments and critical manipulation steps. 5.5.2 EVALUATION RESULTS Table 10: Real-World evluation. We report task success rate over 20 episodes per task, with 10 trials in domain and the other 10 trials out-of-domain. As shown in Table 10, we compare NEO-VLA with π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025) and StarVLA (StarVLA Community, 2026) using the same real-world training data and each methods recommended post-training setup. Task 1 and Task 3 emphasize precise object interaction and placement, while Task 2 requires sustained long-horizon execution across multiple sequential manipulation steps. NEO-VLA achieves the strongest overall performance after the same fine-tuning process, with success rates of 12/20, 17/20, and 13/20 across three real-world tasks. It substantially outperforms StarVLA and matches or exceeds π0.5 in every setting, despite its smaller model scale. More importantly, NEO-VLA maintains strong performance when object configurations deviate from those seen during training, indicating that the learned policy captures transferable visual-action structure rather than simply memorizing demonstrated layouts. The qualitative examples in Figure 6 further illustrate this capability across diverse interaction patterns, including precise placement, object reorientation, sequential manipulation, and multi-step execution. Taken together, these results show that the native VLA design transfers effectively to real-world control, supporting both fine-grained manipulation and long-horizon behavior under limited real-world supervision, while retaining robustness to changes in the observed scene. 3B 1/20 0/20 StarVLA π0.5 3B 10/20 14/20 13/20 NEO-VLA 2B 12/20 17/20 13/20 Size Task1 Task2 Task3 Model 2/20 11 5.5.

sections.title: INFERENCE LATENCY
sections.content: Stage Table 11: Inference latency summary. We report milliseconds per query on one RTX 3090 in BF16, with raw 30-step chunks. We also measure latency on the real robot (pika), with the policy served on single NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB) in bf16. Each query returns one raw 30-step action chunk, which we execute as predicted without real-time chunking (Black et al., 2026). Table 11 reports our default of 10 Euler steps and, for reference, 2-step setting. With 10 steps, compiled forward pass takes 282.5 ms. Most of it goes to the action expert, whose 10 Euler steps take 163.4 ms. The backbone prefix pass takes 84.8 ms and runs only once per query, since every step reuses its keyvalue cache. The convolutional patch embedder costs 3.1ms. Compiling the backbone and expert layers with torch.compile, together with caching the conditioning inputs within each request, cuts the forward pass from 515.4 to 282.5ms and changes predicted positions by at most 0.002cm. On the robot, query takes 261.9 ms from request to the returned chunk, and 286.2ms until an executable plan is ready after inverse kinematics. Cutting sampling to 2 steps shortens the expert to 32.4ms and the full query to 178.5ms, so the prefix pass becomes the main cost. Fewer steps also change the sampled actions; note that all success rates in Table 10 use 10 steps. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: NEO-VLA challenges common assumption in modern VLA design: that action should operate on visual representations already distilled for semantic understanding. Our results instead suggest that effective control benefits from retaining access to the visual computation before it collapses into final semantic representation. native backbone is already highly transferable to action when frozen, early-layer access is consistently valuable, and simply exposing an encoder-based VLM to intermediate visual features does not recover the same benefit. This indicates that what matters is not encoder removal alone, but how visual representations are formed and exposed to the policy throughout the backbone. The broader picture is equally revealing. NEO-VLA is highly robust when the appearance or observation of scene changes, yet remains challenged when the spatial configuration or task goal itself changes. This asymmetry suggests that the next bottleneck in embodied intelligence may no longer be perception alone, but converting perceptual understanding into flexible action under changing geometry and intent. We therefore view native VLA modeling as step toward representations that are not only semantically meaningful, but intrinsically useful for control.
